It is the #39 rfissa's Algerian cousin in the soaked-bread canon, the mountain's own version run with the fierce tomato-chile rougag's register, and the dish that eastern Algeria serves to every assembly worth feeding.

skeleton:
Chakhchoukha Ravioli Stew

Algerian · Medium · Serves 6

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Chakhchoukha is the Aurès mountains' great gathering dish: rougag — paper-thin flatbreads cooked on a pan for seconds — torn to fragments and dried, then soaked at the table in a rich lamb-and-vegetable stew that is poured over until the bread drinks the broth and the whole platter becomes one shared, steaming mass. It is the #39 rfissa's Algerian cousin in the soaked-bread canon, the mountain's own version run with the fierce tomato-chile rougag's register, and the dish that eastern Algeria serves to every assembly worth feeding.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The rougag (the torn bread base — or the bridge)

  • a batter-thin dough
  • or the #39's honest everyman, day-old khobz

The stew

- **Make the rougag a day ahead — the drying is the soaking's law.** The batter-thin dough is ladled by the spoonful onto the dry medium pan for 20–30 seconds a side — no browning, only the leaf's set — and the stacked leaves, dried overnight and torn, become the chakhchoukha's base: fragments that drink the stew without dissolving to paste. The fresh-torn leaf soaks to glue; the dried fragments hold their chew. - **The bridge:** the store trid runs honestly (the diaspora's own working truth), and the day-old bread runs the everyman's register — the soaked-base canon's economy holds through all three roads.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The rougag: paper-thin, cooked to the mere set, dried and torn.
  • The stew: the tremble's 2 hours, the broth generous and one notch past salted.
  • The soak: at the platter, strained broth first, the table eating as the bread drinks.

Chakhchoukha Ravioli Stew

Prep: 1 hour 30 minutes (the rougag ahead) · Cook: 2 hours · Total: About 3 hours 30 minutes · Serves 6

Ingredients

The rougag (the torn bread base — or the bridge)

  • 400 g flour; ½ tsp salt; 450 ml water (approximately) — a batter-thin dough
  • A flat pan at medium heat; the leaves cooked by the spoonful for seconds each, stacked, dried an hour (or overnight), and torn to fragments
  • The bridge: 300 g store trid or mille-feuille pastry, torn — or the #39's honest everyman, day-old khobz

The stew

  • 800 g lamb (shoulder or shank), cut to 5 cm pieces
  • 3 tbsp neutral oil (about 40 g); 2 onions (about 300 g), one grated and one sliced
  • 4 cloves garlic (about 15 g), sliced; 1 tbsp tomato paste (about 15 g)
  • 2 tsp paprika (about 5 g); 1 tbsp dried-mint or parsley flakes or a fist of fresh parsley (about 15 g); 1 tsp cumin; 1 tsp chile flakes (the mountain's honest hand)
  • 1 tsp salt; 2 litres water; 200 g chickpeas, soaked 8 hours
  • 3 tomatoes (about 300 g), grated; 2 potatoes (about 250 g), in large pieces; 2 carrots (about 200 g), thick-coined; 1 zucchini (about 150 g), halved (the mountain pot's row)
  • A fist of cilantro (about 15 g) at the finish; the #91 harissa thinned, at the table

Instructions

  1. **The stew's long base (1 hour 30 minutes).** Brown the lamb in the oil; the onions, the garlic, the tomato paste, and the spices 3 minutes to the perfume; the grated tomatoes, the chickpeas, and the water — brought to a bare simmer, covered, and trembled (95 °C) 1 hour. Checkpoint — the broth at the hour: deep red-brown, the paprika's warmth and the chile's honest hand running through, the chickpeas tender. The lamb approaching its yield — 30 minutes more with the vegetables will finish it.
  2. **The vegetables' entry (30 minutes).** The potatoes and carrots in; 20 minutes; the zucchini for the last 10 — each to its own tenderness, holding. The salt's final taste: the broth must run one notch past comfort (the dry bread's fragments will calm it at the soak). Checkpoint — the finished stew: a rich, moderately thick body — the vegetables' shapes held, the broth coat-the-spoon but pourable (this is a soaking stew, not a glaze: the broth's measure is the base's drink, and it must be generous).
  3. **The soak — the platter's theater (5 minutes).** The torn, dried rougag fragments spread deep across the great platter; a ladle of the broth (strained of its solids) poured over and worked through the fragments with the ladle's edge; the lamb and the vegetables' ring over; and the remaining broth poured at the table until the platter's edge drinks — the diners eating as the bread drinks, the mass softening from the edges in. Checkpoint — eating test, by spoon from the shared platter: the soaked fragments' chew — softened but still holding their texture, the dried bread's honest resistance — carrying the broth's deep, mountain-hot savor, a lamb piece and a vegetable in the same scoop, the cilantro's green and the harissa's fire at the table's dial. It should taste like the assembly's own food: one platter, one bread, one stew, and the mountain's argument that this — not the plate — is how a feast is served.

Finish & Plate

The great platter to the table's center — the fragments' mass under the lamb and the vegetables' ring, the broth's ladle at the diner's hand — spoons for every hand, the harissa and cilantro at the table, and the assembly's own service: everyone from the one expanse.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Bread dissolved to pasteFresh leaf, not driedThe overnight drying \u2014 the chew's law
Platter dry at its centerBroth under-ladledThe broth's measure is generous \u2014 pour at the table
Stew's fire one-notePaprika forward, herbs shyThe parsley and cilantro's green counter

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The stew keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves (the standing pot); the rougag keeps a week dried in cloth. The soak is always at the meal. The #39 rfissa is this record's Moroccan cousin in the soaked canon. - Variations: the chicken version, the dried-buttermilk (lben) drizzle of the mountain's winter service. The #25 and #54's stuffing crafts are the canon's siblings; this record is the platter's own.
